beats.text: Right now, in a factory in Japan, the lights are off.
beats.dir: quiet, intriguing hook, almost a whisper

beats.text: Nobody is inside. And the machines are still building… more machines.
beats.dir: slow reveal, a little eerie

beats.text: FANUC has run factories like this since 2001. Its robots can work for up to thirty days without a human checking on them.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So here's the question everyone is quietly asking: if robots can work in the dark, do they still need us?
beats.dir: curious, direct question to the viewer

beats.text: The answer is stranger than yes or no. And it starts with a machine you probably used last week.
beats.dir: teasing, confident

beats.text: First, the scale. At the end of 2025, about five million industrial robots were working in factories around the world. A new record.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: In 2025 alone, factories installed more than six hundred thousand new ones.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: China installed fifty-nine percent of them. More than the rest of the world combined.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And India? About ten thousand five hundred in a single year. Another record, and sixth in the world.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Outside factories, Amazon says it now runs more than one million robots across its warehouse network.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Internal documents reported by The New York Times suggest automation could let Amazon avoid hiring about six hundred thousand people by 2033.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Amazon says those papers reflect one team, not its hiring plan.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So yes, the robots are real, and they're multiplying. But here's what the headlines miss.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Robots are brilliant at things we find hard… and terrible at things we find easy.
beats.dir: turning point, lean in

beats.text: A robot arm can weld a car door in seconds, exactly the same way, thousands of times a day.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: But ask it to fold a towel, or find one sock in a messy laundry basket, and it struggles.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Scientists call this Moravec's paradox. Seeing, grasping, walking through a cluttered room: the skills evolution spent millions of years building are the hardest ones to copy.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: That's why the new humanoid robots, the ones shaped like people, still do narrow jobs. Moving boxes. Loading metal parts. Carrying totes.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Figure's humanoids spent months loading sheet-metal parts at a BMW plant in the US. Agility says its robot, Digit, has moved more than a hundred thousand totes in a warehouse.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Impressive. But a long way from replacing a mechanic, a nurse or an electrician.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Now, that machine you used last week. The ATM.
beats.dir: playful callback

beats.text: When ATMs arrived, people said bank tellers were finished. A machine that hands out cash all day, with no lunch break.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: What actually happened? ATMs made each branch cheaper to run. So banks opened more branches.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Each branch needed fewer tellers. But there were many more branches.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: In the US, teller jobs didn't collapse. By 2018 there were more tellers than in 2000.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And the job changed. Less counting cash. More helping customers, selling loans, solving problems.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Economists see this pattern again and again: machines take over tasks, not whole jobs.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: But here's the twist. The story didn't end there.
beats.dir: twist, slow down

beats.text: Today, the World Economic Forum lists bank tellers among the fastest-declining jobs on the planet. Not because of the ATM. Because of the phone in your pocket.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: In India you already know what that looks like: you scan a QR code, and you never meet a cashier at all.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So the lesson isn't "technology never takes jobs". It's this: the first machine rarely kills a job. The next one can.
beats.dir: firm, memorable line

beats.text: So what do the big studies predict?
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The World Economic Forum surveyed more than a thousand of the world's largest employers.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Their forecast: by 2030, about ninety-two million jobs displaced… and one hundred and seventy million new ones created.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: That's a net gain of seventy-eight million jobs. But a global total hides millions of people forced to switch careers.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The roles shrinking fastest: cashiers, clerks, data entry, bank tellers.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The roles growing fastest: AI and machine learning specialists, big data specialists, fintech engineers.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And the biggest growth in raw numbers? Not tech at all. Farmworkers, delivery drivers, construction workers.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The IMF adds another angle: almost forty percent of jobs worldwide are exposed to AI. In rich countries, about sixty percent.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Exposed doesn't mean replaced. The IMF says roughly half of those jobs could benefit, because AI makes the worker more productive.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The other half could see less hiring and lower pay.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So what does this mean for India?
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: India's factories are automating fast, mostly car plants. Automotive takes almost half of India's new industrial robots.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: But India's biggest job engine isn't the assembly line. It's services. IT, customer support, back office.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And that's exactly where AI, not robots, is moving in. Software that writes code, answers tickets and reads documents.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: It's the ATM pattern again: the routine tasks go first. Checking, copying, sorting, repeating.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The work that stays is the work around the machine: designing it, fixing it, checking what it produces, and dealing with people.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So, will robots replace human jobs?
beats.dir: reflective, the big question

beats.text: Some, yes. A job that is one repetitive task from start to finish is in real danger.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: But most jobs are a bundle of tasks. Machines take the predictable ones, and leave the messy, human ones.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Remember that dark factory in Japan? Someone designed those robots. Someone programs them. And when one breaks down at three in the morning, a human still gets the call.
beats.dir: warm callback to the opening

beats.text: So the better question isn't "Will a robot take my job?" It's "Which part of my job could a robot do… and what will I do instead?"
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Answer that before your boss does, and you're already ahead.
beats.dir: confident, upbeat

beats.text: Subscribe to TechDecoded with Max for more tech, decoded.
beats.dir: friendly sign-off
